procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated the 7th December, 1982 of the Kerala High Court in Election Petition No. 8 of 1982 dismissing the election petition.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant (original petitioner) filed an election petition in the Kerala High Court challenging the election of respondent No. 1 as a member of the Kerala Legislative Assembly. The appellant alleged corrupt practices and irregularities in the counting of ballot papers. The High Court (Election Judge) dismissed the election petition, rejecting the charges of corrupt practices and irregularities in counting, and also rejected a request for a recount.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant, having lost in the High Court, appealed to the Supreme Court under Section 116A of the Representation of People Act, 1951. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, affirming the High Court's decision.

directions: Parties shall beat their own costs in this Court.

issue.issue_text: Whether the election of the respondent was vitiated by corrupt practices under Section 123(4) of the Representation of the People Act.

facts: The appellant challenged the respondent's election, alleging a corrupt practice under Section 123(4) of the Representation of the People Act.

The specific allegation was that the respondent's election agent published and distributed a hand-bill containing false and serious statements about the appellant's personal character, namely that he had caused the murder of a female political worker.
law: The Court affirmed the legal principle that a charge of corrupt practice in an election case must be proven beyond a reasonable doubt.
This standard of proof is the same as that required in a criminal case.
application: The Supreme Court noted that the High Court had already appreciated the evidence and the witnesses.
It found that the High Court had correctly applied the high standard of proof (beyond a reasonable doubt) to the evidence and concluded that the allegations of corrupt practice had not been proven.
The Supreme Court stated that since the High Court applied the right legal standard, it would not re-appreciate the evidence itself.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court was correct in rejecting the challenge to the election. It held that the appellant had failed to prove the charge of corrupt practice to the required standard of 'proof beyond a reasonable doubt', and therefore, the respondent's election was not vitiated.

issue.issue_text: Whether there were irregularities in the counting of ballot papers that would justify a direction for a recount.

facts: The appellant alleged there were irregularities in the counting of ballot papers.
The High Court had previously rejected a request for a recount.
law: To justify a direction for a recount, the necessary details must be pleaded in the election petition.
Cogent material (strong evidence) must be presented to the court to justify a recount.
application: The Supreme Court found that the appellant had not pleaded the necessary details for a recount in the election petition.
The Court also found that the appellant had not presented any cogent material that would justify ordering a recount.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the plea for a recount because the appellant failed to properly plead the necessary details in the petition and did not provide any compelling evidence to the court.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the election of the respondent was vitiated by corrupt practices under Section 123(4) of the Representation of the People Act.
appellant_arguments: The appellant presented oral evidence from their own workers (PWs 7, 8, 11, and 12) to prove that the respondent had published objectionable materials.
The appellant tried to use a police officer's (P.W.4) report, which mentioned the propaganda, as evidence.
The appellant justified not summoning the printer of the materials by claiming the press had already issued a denial and would not have cooperated.
respondent_arguments: The appellant's witnesses were biased, being their own political workers, and their testimony was not credible or sufficient to establish the charge.
The appellant failed to produce primary evidence by not taking legal steps to enforce the production of documents from the printer.
The police officer's report was inadmissible hearsay and could not be relied upon.

arguments.issue_text: Whether there were irregularities in the counting of ballot papers that would justify a direction for a recount.
appellant_arguments: The appellant alleged that there were irregularities in the counting of ballot papers.

cases.case_name: Mahant Sliree Nath v. Chaudhry 'Ranbir Singh
cases.principle: A charge of corrupt practice under the Representation of the People Act must be established by clear and cogent evidence and proved beyond a reasonable doubt, with the standard of proof being the same as in a criminal case.
When a High Court has appreciated the evidence and found that an allegation of corrupt practice has not been proved, the Supreme Court would not re-appreciate the evidence.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A charge of corrupt practice under the Representation of the People Act has to be proved beyond a reasonable doubt, and the standard of proof is the same as in a criminal case.
obiter: When a High Court has applied the right standard in the matter of appreciation of the material placed before it and has come to hold that the allegations of corrupt practice have not been proved, the Supreme Court will not re-appreciate the evidence.

Workers at an election with party alignment are political supporters of the respective candidates, and when called as witnesses, they would support their stand, with instances not being uncommon where such witnesses support their candidates even if the case is far from the truth.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Court concluded that the High Court was correct to reject the challenge to the respondent's election. The appellant failed to prove the charge of corrupt practice to the high standard required—beyond a reasonable doubt—as the oral testimony came from biased political workers and the documentary evidence was inadmissible hearsay. Furthermore, the appellant did not provide the necessary pleadings or cogent material to justify a recount of the ballots.
legal_tests_applied: A charge of corrupt practice under the Representation of the People Act has to be proved beyond reasonable doubt, and the standard of proof is the same as in a criminal case.
To justify a direction for a recount, the necessary details must be pleaded in the election petition and cogent material must be placed before the Court.
When the High Court has applied the right standard of proof and appreciated the material, the Supreme Court would not re-appreciate the evidence.
why_appellant_lost: The oral testimony of the appellant's witnesses (PWs 7, 8, 11, and 12) was insufficient because they were admittedly workers of the appellant, and in a politically divided election, such witnesses are expected to support their candidate's case even if it is 'far from truth'.

The appellant attempted to rely on a police officer's report which the court deemed inadmissible hearsay 'of a type to which no credence could attach,' and the appellant's counsel could not cite any legal basis for its admission.
The appellant failed to plead the necessary details or present any cogent material in the election petition that would justify a court-ordered recount of the ballots.
why_respondent_won: The evidence presented by the appellant did not meet the high standard of proof required for a charge of corrupt practice, which is equivalent to that of a criminal case (beyond a reasonable doubt).
The High Court had already correctly appreciated the evidence and applied the proper legal standards, and the Supreme Court deferred to this finding.
The plea for a recount was correctly negatived by the High Court because it was not properly substantiated with necessary pleadings or evidence.
policy_considerations: The court recognizes that in elections fought on party lines with sharp political divisions, witnesses who are political workers for a candidate are inherently biased and their testimony is often unreliable. The court notes, 'Instances are not uncommon where such witnesses support their respective candidates and their cases even though the same be far from truth.'
